sites.text: A lattice tower is an open steel framework with a wide base and no guy wires.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1a (macro structures): PTTG, Connecticut Siting Council; looks only
sites.look: open criss-cross steel frame, wide at the bottom, narrowing up

sites.text: A guyed mast is a slim mast held up by cables that run to anchors in the ground, so it needs a big patch of land.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1a (macro structures): PTTG, Connecticut Siting Council; looks only
sites.look: thin mast with long cables slanting to the ground

sites.text: A monopole is one tapered steel column with the antennas near the top.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1a (macro structures): PTTG, Connecticut Siting Council; looks only
sites.look: a single smooth pole, thicker at the bottom

sites.text: A rooftop site puts the antennas on the roof or edge of a building.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1c (building-mounted sites): ALB law firm, Raycap concealment guide; looks only
sites.look: antennas on a building edge or roof

sites.text: Some sites put the antennas around a water tank, or on a tower beside it.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md Gaps section: no source found for water-tank designs (only a San Diego water-tower look-alike, section 1c); so UNVERIFIED until one is found
sites.look: antennas ringed on a water tank

sites.text: A stealth site hides its antennas inside a disguise, such as a fake tree (monopine), palm (monopalm), flagpole or steeple.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1d: PTTG, BroadbandSearch, local planning codes; looks only
sites.look: a tree, palm, flagpole or steeple shape that is too tidy to be real

sites.text: A small cell is a small radio on a pole or building, with a canister or shroud up high and a radio box or cabinet lower down. It reaches a small area.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1e: municipal small-cell design standards; looks only
sites.look: canister or shroud on a street or utility pole, box or cabinet below

sites.text: A DAS is many small antennas inside or on a big venue such as a stadium. One system is often shared by several carriers.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1f: telecoms.com, RCR Wireless (2015); pages not opened here
sites.look: small antennas spread around a venue, sometimes behind fake vents

sites.text: A COW is a cell site on a trailer; a COLT is built onto a vehicle. They run on generators and link back by satellite or microwave. FirstNet is AT&T's public-safety network and runs SatCOLTs and SatCOWs.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1g: FirstNet Deployables PDF (https://www.firstnet.gov/sites/default/files/FirstNet_Deployables.pdf); not opened here
sites.look: trailer or truck with a telescoping mast, a generator and a dish

sites.text: A tower taller than 200 ft (60.96 m) above the ground must be registered with the FCC (ASR). A tower near an airport flight path may need it at any height.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1b: FCC ASR help (https://www.fcc.gov/node/23343), Wikipedia ASR page; pages not opened here

sites.text: The registration (ASR) number must be posted where the public can see it, near the base of the tower.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1b: 47 CFR 17.4(g), Kelley Drye advisory, Federal Register 2024-02871; the note says the exact current eCFR wording was not confirmed

sites.text: A structure taller than 200 ft should normally be marked with orange-and-white paint and/or lights, under FAA rules. The FAA can also ask for marking on shorter structures because of where they stand.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1b: FAA FAQ (https://www.faa.gov/faq/what-are-requirements-aircraft-warning-lights-tall-structures); page not opened here

sites.text: A tower with orange-and-white paint or warning lights is very likely taller than 200 ft, or near an airport. Plain galvanized steel with no lights is more likely shorter. This is a good guess, not a law.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md Inferences section (lesson anchor, marked there as probable, not certain), built on rules rule:asr-200ft and rule:faa-marking

sites.text: Signs at the foot of a tower typically include the registration (ASR) sign, a radio-wave (RF) warning sign and a no-trespassing sign.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1h: Trident Solutions (vendor); typical, not required everywhere

sites.text: Tower companies such as American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge and Array own many towers and rent space on them to the carriers. The owner and the carrier are often not the same company.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1h (tower owner companies and signage): Inside Towers, Array 8-K, Wilson Amplifiers, ModemGuides

sites.text: A sign at a tower base can give a phone number for problems. That number belongs to the owner of the structure, not always to the carrier on it.
sites.source: docs/research/notes/sites_and_carriers.md section 1h (tower owner companies and signage): Inside Towers, Array 8-K, Wilson Amplifiers, ModemGuides

sites.text: When working out who runs a site, the carrier's own sticker counts most and the equipment brand counts least.
sites.source: docs/PRD.md section 4 (chain of evidence); app design rule, not a public fact

hardware.text: A passive panel antenna is a tall plastic cover with no electronics inside. Its cable connectors sit in a row at the bottom.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: The Antenna Farm (SBNHH-1D65C, NNHH-65C-R4 listings), Argus/CommScope model-number chart (Scribd); resellers, pages not opened here

hardware.text: A radio unit (RRU or RRH, a remote radio head) is a small box that makes the signal. Short cables, called jumpers, link it to the connectors of a passive panel.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: fccid.io / device.report (Samsung RF4440d-13A, FCC ID A3LRF4440D-13A), Ericsson Radio 4449 overview; pages not opened here

hardware.text: A massive MIMO box has the radio and a big array of small antennas (about 128 to 192) in one box. It usually has no jumpers to a separate panel. These boxes serve fast mid-band (TDD) spectrum such as n41, n77 and CBRS.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: Montgomery County MD filings (AIR 6449 B77D), fccid.io VBNAEHC-01 (Nokia AEHC), CT Griswold filing (Samsung MT6407-77A), Telecoms.com (AIR 3268); pages not opened here

hardware.text: Massive MIMO boxes often sit on their own support pipe next to the passive panels of the same sector.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: Montgomery County MC2021061469 (AIR 6449 B41 installed on new support pipes for sectors 2 and 3); page not opened here

hardware.text: A hexport panel (like the SBNHH) has 6 connectors. We have not checked how they split between low and mid band.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: The Antenna Farm (SBNHH-1D65C, NNHH-65C-R4 listings), Argus/CommScope model-number chart (Scribd); resellers, pages not opened here

hardware.text: An NNHH panel has 8 connectors: 4 for low band and 4 for mid band.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: The Antenna Farm (SBNHH-1D65C, NNHH-65C-R4 listings), Argus/CommScope model-number chart (Scribd); resellers, pages not opened here

hardware.text: A band that works as 4T4R needs 4 antenna ports, so counting a band's ports usually tells you its T and R number. This is a good guess from how the panels are built, not a law.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3 (inference from the panel and radio listings above)

hardware.text: In a CommScope panel name, the last letter is the length: A is 1.3 m, B is 2.0 m and C is 2.6 m. In the band letters, N means 698 to 896 MHz and H means 1710 to 2180 MHz.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: The Antenna Farm (SBNHH-1D65C, NNHH-65C-R4 listings), Argus/CommScope model-number chart (Scribd); resellers, pages not opened here

hardware.text: Ericsson's AIR means Antenna Integrated Radio. The first two digits of the model number usually match the radio paths: AIR 6449 has 64 (64T64R) and AIR 3268 has 32. This is a pattern in the examples we found, not a law.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: Montgomery County MD filings (AIR 6449 B77D), fccid.io VBNAEHC-01 (Nokia AEHC), CT Griswold filing (Samsung MT6407-77A), Telecoms.com (AIR 3268); pages not opened here; the 'first two digits' rule is our reading of the AIR 6449, AIR 6419 and AIR 3268 examples

hardware.text: The ending of an Ericsson AIR name shows the band: B41 is 2.5 GHz (2496 to 2690 MHz), B77D is C-band (3700 to 3980 MHz) and B48 is CBRS.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: Montgomery County MD filings MC2020061185, MC2021011358, MC2021061469 (Ericsson AIR 6449 B41 / B77D); fccid.io TA8AKRD901206; pages not opened here

hardware.text: A dual-band Ericsson radio lists both bands in its name, such as Radio 4449 B5/B13 or Radio 4480 B71+B85.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: Ericsson Radio 4449 overview, RRUS 4449 B5/B12 spec sheet, CT Sterling filing (Radio 4480 B71+B85, RRUS 8843 B2 B66A); pages not opened here

hardware.text: Nokia's AEHC is the AirScale MAA 64T64R 192AE B41: a 64T64R massive MIMO box for band 41.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: fccid.io VBNAEHC-01, Nokia Massive MIMO Adaptive Antenna Product Description; pages not opened here

hardware.text: Samsung names may end in the band: -77A for n77 and -13A for band 13. This is only our guess from two examples.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2 inference only: the -77A and -13A endings are our reading of two Samsung names; no Samsung document explains them

hardware.text: T-Mobile's filings list the Ericsson AIR 6449 B41, so it is a T-Mobile n41 (2.5 GHz) radio.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: Montgomery County MD filings MC2021011358, MC2021061469, MC2021111611, MC2020101317 (T-Mobile, AIR 6449 B41); pages not opened here

hardware.text: The Ericsson AIR 6449 B77D is a C-band radio. AT&T is named in its filings. Verizon's C-band uses Samsung boxes in the filings we found.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: Montgomery County MD filings MC2020061185, MC2021011358, MC2021061469 (Ericsson AIR 6449 B41 / B77D); fccid.io TA8AKRD901206; pages not opened here

hardware.text: Verizon's filings list the Samsung MT6407-77A (a 64T64R C-band all-in-one) and the Samsung RF4440d-13A (a 700/850 MHz radio).
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: Montgomery County MC2022051756, CT Griswold filing em-ver-058-211018 (Samsung MT6407-77A, RF4440d-13A); pages not opened here

hardware.text: A T-Mobile tower-share notice lists the Ericsson Radio 4480 B71+B85, a dual-band radio that includes the 600 MHz band 71.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 2: CT Sterling T-Mobile tower-share notice (Radio 4480 B71+B85); the AT&T Clinton notice is ambiguous and is not used; page not opened here

hardware.text: Massive MIMO boxes have got lighter with each generation. Very roughly, a big one is about 25 to 40 kg and a small one about 12 kg. Sources disagree on exact weights.
hardware.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 3: The Mobile Network (AIR 6468), Nokia (Habrok 64, 24 kg), Telecoms.com (AIR 3268, 12 kg); one reseller says 46 kg for the B41 AIR 6449, which conflicts with the filings (35 to 38 kg)

hardware.text: A radio's model name usually tells you what the box is, but not always who runs it. The carrier's own sticker counts most and the equipment brand counts least.
hardware.source: docs/PRD.md section 4 (chain of evidence); app design rule, not a public fact

cell_ids.text: Cells come in size classes, from widest to smallest: macro (wide area, on towers above the rooftops), micro (medium range, below the rooftops), pico (local area, such as inside a mall) and femto (home). Home cells exist only in LTE, not in 5G.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 4: Techplayon LTE and NR base-station classes, ScienceDirect overview; pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: A site usually has 3 sectors, each facing about a third of a circle. Each band on each sector is its own cell, so the number of cells is roughly the number of sectors times the number of bands. This is a good rule of thumb, not a law.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 4: Montgomery County filing MC2021061469 (sectors numbered), MIT cellular numerology page; pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: An LTE cell number (the ECI) is 28 bits: 20 bits are the tower (eNB) number and 8 bits are the cell number. So ECI = eNB x 256 + cell, and eNB = ECI divided by 256 (rounded down).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: US Patent 8346280 (20-bit eNB ID, 8-bit cell), HowardForums 'LTE sectors' (ECI = eNB x 256 + sector); pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: An LTE PCI (physical cell ID) is a number from 0 to 503. Cells reuse PCIs, so a PCI tells you neither the site nor the band.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: MIT cellular numerology page, Cellfire app on GitHub (PCI 0 to 503); pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: A channel number (EARFCN) gives the exact frequency: the downlink frequency in MHz = the band's lowest downlink frequency + 0.1 x (channel number - the band's first channel number).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GPP TS 36.101 Table 5.7.3-1 as copied by Halberd Bastion, Electronics Notes, CableFree, Wikipedia LTE frequency bands, celltowers.ca; the ranges also match content/bands.json (a test checks); not yet compared with 3GPP itself (T07)

cell_ids.text: Band 12 downlink channel numbers run from 5010 to 5179 (729 to 746 MHz).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GPP TS 36.101 Table 5.7.3-1 as copied by Halberd Bastion, Electronics Notes, CableFree, Wikipedia LTE frequency bands, celltowers.ca; the ranges also match content/bands.json (a test checks); not yet compared with 3GPP itself (T07)

cell_ids.text: Band 13 downlink channel numbers run from 5180 to 5279 (746 to 756 MHz).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GPP TS 36.101 Table 5.7.3-1 as copied by Halberd Bastion, Electronics Notes, CableFree, Wikipedia LTE frequency bands, celltowers.ca; the ranges also match content/bands.json (a test checks); not yet compared with 3GPP itself (T07)

cell_ids.text: Band 66 downlink channel numbers run from 66436 to 67335 (2110 to 2200 MHz).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GPP TS 36.101 Table 5.7.3-1 as copied by Halberd Bastion, Electronics Notes, CableFree, Wikipedia LTE frequency bands, celltowers.ca; the ranges also match content/bands.json (a test checks); not yet compared with 3GPP itself (T07)

cell_ids.text: Band 71 downlink channel numbers run from 68586 to 68935 (617 to 652 MHz).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GPP TS 36.101 Table 5.7.3-1 as copied by Halberd Bastion, Electronics Notes, CableFree, Wikipedia LTE frequency bands, celltowers.ca; the ranges also match content/bands.json (a test checks); not yet compared with 3GPP itself (T07)

cell_ids.text: Channel number ranges for the other US LTE bands (B2, B4, B5, B14, B17, B25, B30, B41, B48).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5 gaps: EARFCN ranges for B2, B4, B5, B14, B17, B25, B30, B41 and B48 were not sourced; verify against 3GPP (T07)

cell_ids.text: A 5G cell number (the NCI) is 36 bits. The first 22 to 32 bits are the tower (gNB) number and the rest are the cell number. The screen does not say where the split is, so a drill always states the bit length.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: Techplayon NR cell global identity planning, 5G-Tools NCI calculator, arXiv 2506.12461; pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: We did not find how many bits any US carrier uses for the tower number in 5G. The same 5G cell number decodes to two different sites if you assume two different lengths.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5 gaps: no source found for any US carrier's gNB ID length (UK examples exist only as community posts)

cell_ids.text: A 5G PCI is a number from 0 to 1007.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5 (PCI range for 5G not covered); the value 0 to 1007 is a 3GPP standard figure we recalled and did not source, so it stays UNVERIFIED until T07

cell_ids.text: A 5G channel number (NR-ARFCN) also maps to an exact frequency, by one global formula with a fixed step size. Learners only need the idea, not the formula.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: 3GLTEInfo, nrarfcn on PyPI (3GPP TS 38.104 section 5.4.2.1); concept only; pages not opened here

cell_ids.text: Community pattern, may have changed: on Verizon, the tens digit of the LTE cell number often shows the sector and the ones digit shows the layer (for example 1, 2 and 3 are often 700 MHz).
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: S4GRU posts (Trip) and HowardForums Verizon B2 PCS thread; forum posts only, two agree; may have changed

cell_ids.text: Community pattern, may have changed: T-Mobile cell numbers often group by band, such as band 66 in 1 to 10, band 2 in 11 to 20 and band 71 in 61 to 70, with exceptions.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: S4GRU 'How to Identify T-Mobile network equipment (Nokia Networks)'; one forum post with stated exceptions; may have changed

cell_ids.text: A vendor name that a map app shows next to a cell number is a guess from the number's pattern, so do not trust it.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 5: HowardForums 'who is the vendor of this cell equipment' (CellMapper and LTE Discovery 'just make a best guess'); forum post

cell_ids.text: On many iPhones, dialling a Field Test code opens a hidden test screen that shows the cell number and PCI. The menus differ by iOS version and phone, so yours may look different.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 6: iTechGuides, FindCellID, UberSignal, Wilson (iPhone Field Test); web guides, not tried on a real phone by us

cell_ids.text: On many Android phones, a hidden test code shows the channel number (EARFCN) next to the serving cell. Some phones block it or show other screens.
cell_ids.source: docs/research/notes/vendors_and_cells.md question 6: HiCellTek EARFCN guide, XDA ServiceMode threads; web and forum posts, not tried by us

questions.title: A band is a numbered stretch
questions.text: Radio waves wiggle at different speeds. A band is a stretch of those speeds with a number for a name, like a lane on a road. We count the speed in MHz (megahertz). B71 sits low on the ruler: its downlink runs from {band:B71.dl_low_mhz} to {band:B71.dl_high_mhz} MHz. n258 sits far up at {band:n258.dl_low_mhz} MHz.

questions.title: B is 4G, n is 5G
questions.text: A band that starts with "B" is 4G (also called LTE). A band that starts with "n" is 5G (also called NR). B71 and n71 are twins: they use exactly the same space ({band:B71.dl_low_mhz} to {band:B71.dl_high_mhz} MHz downlink).

questions.prompt: Which is the higher frequency, 2000 MHz or 2 GHz?
questions.why: 1 GHz (gigahertz) is 1000 MHz, so 2 GHz is 2000 MHz. Same thing, different units.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows "n71". Is that 4G or 5G?
questions.why: Bands starting with "n" are 5G. The bands file lists n71 as {band:n71.kind}, a 5G band.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows "B66". Is that 4G or 5G?
questions.why: Bands starting with "B" are 4G. The bands file lists B66 as {band:B66.kind}.

questions.prompt: Match each 4G band to its 5G twin.
questions.why: Twins share the same numbers. Only the letter changes.

questions.prompt: B71 or B66, which one sits higher on the ruler?
questions.why: B66's downlink starts at {band:B66.dl_low_mhz} MHz. B71's starts at {band:B71.dl_low_mhz} MHz.

questions.prompt: Which 4G band is the twin of n25?
questions.why: n25 and B25 share the same numbers. B2 is a close cousin, but not the twin.

questions.prompt: n71 or n41, which one sits higher on the ruler?
questions.why: n41 starts at {band:n41.dl_low_mhz} MHz. n71's downlink starts at {band:n71.dl_low_mhz} MHz.

questions.prompt: n77 or n258, which one sits far higher on the ruler?
questions.why: n258 starts at {band:n258.dl_low_mhz} MHz. n77 starts at {band:n77.dl_low_mhz} MHz.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows "n77". Is that 4G or 5G?
questions.why: Bands starting with "n" are 5G. The bands file lists n77 as {band:n77.kind}.

questions.title: Three parts of the ruler
questions.text: In this app, we split the ruler in three. Low band is any band that starts below 1000 MHz, like B71 ({band:B71.dl_low_mhz} MHz). High band is the very top, called mmWave, like n260 ({band:n260.dl_low_mhz} MHz). Mid band is everything in between, like B2 ({band:B2.dl_low_mhz} MHz). Other people draw the lines a bit differently, so this is the app's own rule.

questions.title: Reach versus speed
questions.text: Low bands are like a deep voice: they travel far and get through walls, but carry less. High bands are like a whisper that moves lots of data: very fast, but they stop at the first wall. Mid bands are in the middle.

questions.prompt: Which part of the ruler is B12 in?
questions.why: B12's downlink starts at {band:B12.dl_low_mhz} MHz, below 1000 MHz, so it is low band.

questions.prompt: Which part of the ruler is B66 in?
questions.why: B66's downlink starts at {band:B66.dl_low_mhz} MHz. That is above 1000 MHz but not mmWave, so it is mid band.

questions.prompt: Which part of the ruler is n41 in?
questions.why: n41 starts at {band:n41.dl_low_mhz} MHz and its kind is {band:n41.kind}, so it is mid band.

questions.prompt: Which part of the ruler is n261 in?
questions.why: n261's kind is {band:n261.kind}. mmWave bands are high band.

questions.prompt: The bands file tags n77 as FR1 or FR2?
questions.why: FR1 is the 5G zone for everything below mmWave. The bands file tags n77 as {band:n77.kind}.

questions.prompt: The bands file tags n260 as FR1 or FR2?
questions.why: FR2 is the mmWave zone. The bands file tags n260 as {band:n260.kind}.

questions.prompt: Put these bands in order, lowest frequency first.
questions.why: Sorted by where each downlink starts, in MHz.

questions.prompt: You are in a basement, far from the tower. Which kind of band helps you most?
questions.why: Low bands travel farthest and get through walls best.

questions.prompt: In this app, a band that starts below what number is low band?
questions.why: The app's rule is 1000 MHz (that is 1 GHz). Below it is low band.

questions.title: Uplink and downlink
questions.text: Uplink is your phone talking to the tower (up). Downlink is the tower talking to your phone (down). Think of a phone call: you speak, then you listen.

questions.title: FDD and TDD
questions.text: FDD is a road with two lanes: one for up, one for down. B2 is FDD: uplink {band:B2.ul_low_mhz} to {band:B2.ul_high_mhz} MHz, downlink {band:B2.dl_low_mhz} to {band:B2.dl_high_mhz} MHz. TDD is a single lane where up and down take turns, very fast. n41 is TDD: one range, {band:n41.dl_low_mhz} to {band:n41.dl_high_mhz} MHz, used both ways.

questions.prompt: Is B12 FDD or TDD?
questions.why: The bands file says B12 is {band:B12.duplex}.

questions.prompt: Is n41 FDD or TDD?
questions.why: The bands file says n41 is {band:n41.duplex}.

questions.prompt: Is B66 FDD or TDD?
questions.why: The bands file says B66 is {band:B66.duplex}. It still has two lanes, just far apart.

questions.prompt: Is n77 FDD or TDD?
questions.why: The bands file says n77 is {band:n77.duplex}.

questions.prompt: n261 is a mmWave band. Is it FDD or TDD?
questions.why: The bands file says n261 is {band:n261.duplex}.

questions.prompt: Which band has one range that is used both ways?
questions.why: That is TDD. n41 is {band:n41.duplex}. B2 and B12 are FDD, with a separate uplink and downlink.

questions.prompt: A band has uplink {band:B2.ul_low_mhz} to {band:B2.ul_high_mhz} MHz and downlink {band:B2.dl_low_mhz} to {band:B2.dl_high_mhz} MHz. FDD or TDD?
questions.why: Two separate ranges means two lanes, which is FDD.

questions.prompt: How far apart are B2's two lanes? Type the gap in MHz.
questions.why: The bands file gives B2's duplex gap as {band:B2.duplex_spacing_mhz} MHz.

questions.prompt: Which part of the ruler is n41 in?

questions.title: Boxes on the tower
questions.text: Up on a tower you will see three kinds of boxes. Think of a speaker setup: a plain speaker, an amplifier, and a speaker with the amplifier built in. The tower has the same three jobs.

questions.title: The plain panel
questions.text: A passive panel antenna is a tall plastic cover with no electronics inside. Its cable connectors sit in a row at the bottom. "Passive" means it only passes the signal along.

questions.title: The radio box
questions.text: A radio unit is a small box that makes the signal. Short cables, called jumpers, link it to the connectors of a passive panel. People also call it an RRU or RRH.

questions.title: The massive MIMO box
questions.text: A massive MIMO box has the radio and a big array of small antennas (about 128 to 192) in one box. It usually has no jumpers to a separate panel.

questions.text: A site is the place with the tower. A sector is one direction, like one slice of a pizza. A cell is one band on one sector. {cellid:cls:sectors.text}

questions.title: Be a detective
questions.text: A detective does not guess. Each clue only narrows things down. Ask four questions in order: what is the frequency, which band is it, who holds that band, and what proof can I see on the ground? Today you practise one clue at a time.

questions.title: Honest answers
